question_text: A 34-year-old man presents with multiple painful ulcers on his penis. He says that the ulcers all appeared suddenly at the same time 3 days ago. He reports that he is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals multiple small shallow ulcers with an erythematous base and without discharge. There is significant inguinal lymphadenopathy present. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent of this patient’s ulcers?

                    ### Question
                    A 34-year-old man presents with multiple painful ulcers on his penis. He says that the ulcers all appeared suddenly at the same time 3 days ago. He reports that he is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals multiple small shallow ulcers with an erythematous base and without discharge. There is significant inguinal lymphadenopathy present. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent of this patient’s ulcers?

                    ### Options

opb. Chlamydia trachomatis
opc. Treponema pallidum
opd. Haemophilus ducreyi
ope. Herpes simplex virus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with multiple painful ulcers on his penis, which appeared suddenly, and significant inguinal lymphadenopathy. Given the sudden onset of multiple ulcers and the sexual history, the most likely etiologic agent is Herpes simplex virus (HSV). HSV typically causes painful, shallow ulcers and can present with lymphadenopathy. The evidence paths confirm that Simplexvirus (HSV) causes painful genital lesions. Other options such as Haemophilus ducreyi, which causes chancroid, typically present with a painful ulcer but often with a purulent base and more localized lymphadenopathy. Treponema pallidum (syphilis) usually presents with a single chancre, making it less likely in the presence of multiple ulcers. Chlamydia trachomatis and Human papillomavirus are unlikely as they typically cause urethritis and genital warts, respectively, not painful ulcers.
